Hello everyone,

I'd like to share a Lean 4 + Mathlib formalization of the nonexistence of a strongly regular graph with parameters (266, 45, 0, 9):

theorem SRG266.srg266_nonexistence {V : Type u} [Fintype V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] :
    ¬ SRG266.IsHypothetical G

Here SRG266.IsHypothetical G is just an abbreviation for

G.IsSRGWith 266 45 0 9

so the theorem directly states that no finite simple graph has these SRG parameters.

As far as I can tell, the existence of SRG(266, 45, 0, 9) was previously open and was listed as unknown in Brouwer's table and other standard SRG parameter tables.

  • Repo: https://github.com/kay-akiyama/srg266-nonexistence-lean (tag v1.0.0)
  • CI (full build + axiom check): https://github.com/kay-akiyama/srg266-nonexistence-lean/actions/runs/32591448762
  • Archived release: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22063604

#print axioms SRG266.srg266_nonexistence reports

[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]

The computational certificates used in the proof are replayed inside Lean using kernel computation via decide.

A proof sketch and details of the formalization are in the README.

Full disclosure: both the mathematics and formalization were LLM-led; details are in the README.

I am a software engineer with no formal background in mathematics, so I'd especially welcome scrutiny of the theorem statement and of whether the intended notion of an SRG has been formalized correctly, as well as any feedback on the proof architecture.

If the result withstands community scrutiny, I would also greatly appreciate advice on appropriate next steps, including arXiv endorsement.

(Note: A full build requires ~140 CPU-hours. For a quick initial audit, python3 scripts/shards.py audit verifies the import closure and certificate dependencies without running the full kernel check.)
Congratulations on this, but which specific LLMs were used?
(It looks like Claude + GPT, similar to https://github.com/Solarys431/lean-eval-platonic-classification)

Thank you!
Yes, it does seem similar.
The mathematical research was led mainly by GPT-5.6 Sol, with Claude Fable 5 used as a second-opinion and discussion partner.
The Lean formalization was done mainly with Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code, with some parts developed using GPT-5.6 Sol + Codex.
